source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: 38 LLMs on Japanese children's riddles (insight-like wordplay) fall far below humans, except the newest model.
numbers: 201 riddles; 120-item human subset, n=126 humans, mean 52.9%. Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6% on subset. Full 201 items: means 9.42% vs 19.25%; pooled odds ratio 2.29 for reasoning. GPT-5 inside human 95% CI.
limits: Zero-shot, no retrieval; no formal model-by-model tests; human sample is an online pilot; Japanese only.
agent_relevance: A renewable insight test set: short riddles, auto-scorable via gold variants. Good S6 candidate; refresh items to keep headroom.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: Parameter count did not predict riddle accuracy; release date did. Human item difficulty is spread out; LLM items pile up near zero.
numbers: 38 models; human score distribution bimodal (peaks at the low end); most items very hard for LLMs.
limits: Correlational across models, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Insight-test scores track training recipe, not size. Test the scaffold on one fixed model, not by scaling.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: Verification failure: the model writes the correct answer in its thinking, then does not commit to it and answers wrongly.
numbers: Share of wrong answers that are verification failures: Gemini-2.5-Flash 5.23%, Claude Opus 4 25.0%, DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57%, Grok 4 39.34% (range 5% to 39%). Test: a gold variant appears literally in the thought log before the final answer.
limits: Literal string match over thought logs (can over- or undercount); only 4 models with usable logs; logs may be unfaithful.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S6: keep every candidate the model ever generates, and let code check candidates against a held-out test before the final choice (G2, G3, G6).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: Language of the thought log (English vs Japanese) did not reliably change accuracy.
numbers: Grok 4: Japanese 29.5% (33/112) vs English 48.8% (40/82), Fisher p=0.0071. Claude Opus 4: 36.7% (16/44) vs 28.7% (45/157), p=0.356. Gemini 2.5 Flash: 0/12 vs 22/188, p=0.369. DeepSeek-R1 used Japanese in 199/199 (23.1%).
limits: Language is chosen by the model per item, so confounded with difficulty.
agent_relevance: Do not spend scaffold budget forcing a reasoning language.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Mid-reasoning 'Wait, let's re-evaluate' shifts are rare and usually do not raise accuracy; they do not match the human aha.
numbers: 1M+ traces, hundreds of checkpoints; Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama 3.1-8B (GRPO-tuned), plus GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 traces; domains: cryptic crosswords, MATH-500, Rush Hour. Shifts in 6.31% of traces. Shifted traces less accurate across models and domains.
limits: Detection by LLM judge plus lexical cues; three detector variants agree. Mostly small open models.
agent_relevance: Surface 'wait' tokens are not an insight signal. The impasse detector must use measured signals (failed check, disagreement), as G1 says.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: A formal 'Aha' (earlier failures, earlier stability, then gain at the shift) almost never occurs.
numbers: Formal detector fires on 1.79% of samples pooled over checkpoints and temperatures; heatmaps under lax thresholds still exceedingly rare.
limits: Definition 3.1 thresholds tuned on a dev slab.
agent_relevance: An operational, checkpoint-level definition of an 'insight event' we could reuse to score S6 results.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Shifts do not become helpful later in training; at T=0.7 they are mildly harmful on crosswords and math.
numbers: Qwen2.5-1.5B: crosswords %S=2.43, AME -0.0311 (p=0.027); math %S=2.17, AME -0.0615; Rush Hour %S=11.4, AME about 0.0001. Math raw gap about -11.8 pp.
limits: Logistic regression with problem fixed effects and cluster-robust SEs.
agent_relevance: Do not let the agent reflect on a schedule (G1). Spontaneous reflection is not free accuracy.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Externally triggering reconsideration when entropy is high gives real gains.
numbers: Paired Pass1 vs Pass2 (appended reconsideration cue): MATH-500 0.322 to 0.406 (+8.41 pp; 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong); crosswords +0.45 pp; Rush Hour +0.01 pp (base rate 0.02%).
limits: Small models; generic cue; crossword and Rush Hour gains near zero.
agent_relevance: Supports 'doubt only on a signal': trigger a recheck from an uncertainty signal as an extrinsic operator, not as self-initiated reflection.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Understanding Aha Moments: from External Observations to Internal Mechanisms
finding: Compares 'aha' reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill) with no-aha math models: aha models use more anthropomorphic self-reflection and adjust uncertainty to difficulty. Proposes the RASM metric.
numbers: Reasoning-collapse (language mixing, repetition) probabilities measured on 200 test samples across difficulty levels; no-aha models keep mean RASM below zero.
limits: Correlational; the comparison confounds aha with distillation and model family; later work (c05-c07) challenges the causal story.
agent_relevance: Shows how insight is measured in LLMs: tone words, uncertainty, latent probes. There is no subjective report. Weak evidence.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026), related-work claims about detectors
finding: The 2026 paper states keyword insight detectors misclassify superficial hesitation as insight at rates up to about 30% in some settings, and that some work finds reflection from epoch 0 of RL training.
numbers: Up to 30% misclassification (cited from other work); reflection at epoch 0.
limits: Secondhand figures; not independently checked.
agent_relevance: Lexical insight detectors are unreliable. Prefer behavioral tests (solve rate on items that need a representation change).

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: A caution against anthropocentrism
finding: Early psychometric battery on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, including the Remote Associates Test (RAT), analytic problems and 5 insight problems.
numbers: RAT: human item pass rates 9% to 85%; GPT-3.5 overall 9% to 45% across 4 sessions; GPT-4 50% and 59% in 2 sessions; item-level human vs GPT-3.5 r=0.39. Insight: human 44% to 61% per item; GPT-3.5 1.5 to 3.5 of 5; GPT-4 4.5 of 5 (one session). Analytic: neither model ever correct on 2 problems (humans 55%, 61%).
limits: Tiny item counts; large run-to-run variability; new chat windows may invalidate; training exposure not ruled out (models asked; no link found).
agent_relevance: Run-to-run variance is large. An S6 test set needs many items and repeated samples.

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: A caution against anthropocentrism
finding: On RAT, models give the right word but a wrong justification (spurious compounds), so answer-only scoring overcounts.
numbers: One GPT-3.5 session: 10 such errors out of 22 triplets, scored as wrong. Examples: 'artist, hatch, route' -> escape; 'river, note, account' -> bank.
limits: Anecdotal examples from one session type.
agent_relevance: Score insight tasks by checking that the answer fits every cue (code check), not by answer match alone (G3).

source: Speed (2023) Assessing the nature of large language models: A caution against anthropocentrism
finding: Measurement lessons: the same model scores differently across sessions; a 'pretend to be human' frame was needed; GPT-4 refused some scales.
numbers: GPT-3.5 insight scores 1.5 to 3.5 of 5 across four sessions; one scale stopped at item 190 after refusals.
limits: Narrative report, tiny n.
agent_relevance: Protocol for our tests: fixed prompts, many repeats, report variance.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT (Jan 9 2023 version) solved about as many verbal insight problems as the human median.
numbers: 30 problems from Ansburg and Dominowski (2000): 15 practice, 15 transfer. ChatGPT 7/15 practice, 5/15 transfer, 12/30 pooled. Humans n=20: practice median 0.55 (IQR 0.23-0.64), transfer 0.35 (0.30-0.40).
limits: One model version; n=20 humans; medians though the abstract says mean; stimuli used but original procedure not replicated; classic items likely in training data.
agent_relevance: Old verbal insight items are contaminated and near human level. Do not use them as the only S6 test.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: The human training protocol was applied to the model: feedback, then control instructions, then strategic instructions.
numbers: Prompts: 'The answer provided is not correct.', then control instructions, then strategic instructions (from Ansburg and Dominowski 2000). Correct: practice #3,6,8,11,13,14,15; transfer #1,6,8,12,13.
limits: Effect of each instruction not isolated.
agent_relevance: A hint-ladder pattern for a test harness: no hint, generic feedback, strategy hint, solution; record which rung unlocks the item.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: Only Connect Wall puzzles (RAT-like with built-in red herrings) test Einstellung in models: GPT-4 is far below humans.
numbers: 494 test walls. Humans solve 285/494 walls and 1405/1976 groups. GPT-4 0-shot: 6 walls, 239 groups; best few-shot (3-shot) 5 walls, 272 groups; GPT-3.5 0-shot 0 walls, 114 groups. Naming the connection: best GPT-4 10-shot F1 41-45% vs human about 80%.
limits: PDF table layout garbled, values read by inference; British quiz-show bias; more in-context examples did not help.
agent_relevance: Red-herring walls are a ready S6 test for fixation and set-breaking. More examples did not help, so the scaffold must do something else.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: Removing red herrings raises model scores a lot, which fits a fixation reading.
numbers: GPT-4 0-shot solved walls: original 6, OCW-Randomized (diluted red herrings) 59, OCW-WordNet (none) 471 (correct groups 239, 595, 1926). GPT-3.5 0-shot: 0, 5, 337 walls.
limits: Synthetic variants differ in more than red herrings (simpler semantics).
agent_relevance: A cheap control for any insight test: build a matched version without the misleading cue; the gap measures fixation.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: Humans vs GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o on creativity tasks, including a Chinese-language RAT and three insight tasks.
numbers: RAT (61 humans, 30 triplets, 1 min each): all three models more accurate than humans (estimates 0.19, 0.26, 0.35; p<0.001). Insight (60 humans): character puzzle, humans beat GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (+0.09) but lost to GPT-4o (-0.21); stumpers, humans beat GPT-3.5 (+0.20) and GPT-4 (+0.06, p=0.014) but lost to GPT-4o (-0.06, p=0.011); rebus, humans lost to GPT-4-turbo (-0.32) and GPT-4o (-0.39).
limits: Chinese students about 20 years old; temperature 0.6-0.8; 60 instances per task; version confound.
agent_relevance: Convergent RAT-like insight is already easy for frontier models. An S6 test needs items whose answer is not a stored association.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: Model answers sit closer to the cue words than human answers.
numbers: RAT semantic-spread measure lower for humans than all models: GPT-3.5 t=-11.46, GPT-4 t=-5.85, GPT-4o t=-12.02 (p<0.001). Story task (63 humans): human stories more diverse and more creative than all three models.
limits: Measure defined by the authors.
agent_relevance: Models stay near the stimulus. Push candidate ideas away from the cue cluster (distant operators) and judge by running.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes (citing Raz 2024, Latif 2024)
finding: The paper cites Raz et al. (2024) as finding GPT-4 significantly better than humans on stumper-type verbal insight, and frames the debate whether that is stored data or real insight.
numbers: No numbers beyond its own experiments.
limits: Raz 2024 and Latif 2024 were not opened by me; treat as cited claims.
agent_relevance: Open question for S6: item novelty. Use fresh items to separate recall from restructuring.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Multiple-choice lateral thinking puzzles (1,100 puzzles, sentence and word types) with semantic and context reconstructions to test consistency; models far below humans.
numbers: Human 91.98% (102 sampled items, 3 experts). ChatGPT overall: sentence 62.68%, word 53.46%; random about 25%. ChatGPT sentence: original 60.77, semantic 59.33, context 67.94; group Ori&Sem 50.72, all three 39.71. About a third of models at or below random.
limits: Memorization seen on word puzzles (ChatGPT recognised 'spell COW in thirteen letters'); 4-option multiple choice; 2023 models; PDF table partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Reconstruction consistency (same puzzle reworded) is a good robustness metric for S6: count an item solved only if all variants pass.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) SemEval-2024 Task 9: BRAINTEASER
finding: Shared task on BRAINTEASER(S): top systems reach 100% on the test subset, yet consistency across rewordings still drops.
numbers: Test split 120 items per subtask; baseline overall: human 0.920, GPT-4 0.898 (full set), ChatGPT 0.627, RoBERTa-L 0.434. Over 80% of leaderboard models drop on Ori&Sem (0.025-0.175 sentence; 0.031-0.281 word); nearly all drop on all-three (0.025-0.275 sentence; 0.031-0.344 word). Fine-tuned systems took ranks 1, 3, 5.
limits: Test set is a 20% subset; 80% was available for training; gains partly from task-specific training.
agent_relevance: Benchmarks saturate once training data exists. Keep a hidden, refreshable set and use consistency across rewordings, not raw accuracy.

source: Tang (2026) BrainBench: Exposing the Commonsense Reasoning Gap in Large Language Models
finding: 100 brainteaser questions in 20 failure-mode categories; 8 frontier models, 10 runs each. The best model still misses about one in five.
numbers: Claude Opus 4.6 with extended thinking 80.3% (consistency 74.0%); Opus 4.6 77.3%; Haiku 4.5 74.3%; GPT-5.4 70.7%; GPT-4o and 4o-mini 39.7%. Hardest categories: implicit physical constraint 40.0%, wrong vantage point 40.0%. Mean accuracy-consistency gap 10.3 pp; GPT-4o-mini 24.0% consistency vs 39.7% accuracy.
limits: Single author, 100 author-written items; mixes commonsense and brainteasers.
agent_relevance: Report accuracy AND consistency over repeated runs for S6. A right answer that appears in only some runs is not a solved item.

source: Tang (2026) BrainBench: Exposing the Commonsense Reasoning Gap in Large Language Models
finding: Extended thinking gives a small average gain on trick questions and hurts in some categories.
numbers: Extended thinking: +3.3 pp GPT-5.4, +3.0 pp Opus 4.6. Gains: pragmatic/social intent +26.7 pp (GPT-5.4), +33.3 pp (Opus). Losses (GPT-5.4 Think): naive physics -26.7 pp, negation logic -13.3 pp.
limits: Per-category n is 5 questions x 10 runs.
agent_relevance: More thinking is not uniformly good (cf. G1: forced doubt hurt our word puzzles, 92% vs 75%). Gate extra thinking by task type.

source: Han et al. (2025) Creativity or Brute Force? Using Brainteasers as a Window into LLM Problem-Solving
finding: Braingle brainteasers (250 hardest math, 250 hardest logic) scored for correctness and for creative vs brute-force route; a hint and a math-style prompt help strong models.
numbers: Math: o3 79.6% CoT, 82.8% with hint, 81.2% math prompt+hint; DeepSeek-R1 66.8 -> 72.4 (hint), 72.8 (both); Gemini-2.5-Flash 66.0 -> 69.2 / 72.0. Logic: o3 68.4 -> 74.4 (both); R1 44.6 -> 50.6. Qwen-1.5B distill flat or worse with hints. o3 as judge agreed with human labels 99.3% and 97%.
limits: Judge is o3 (also a tested model); small-model hint gain absent.
agent_relevance: Hints help strong models only. Route-type scoring (insight vs brute force) is a useful extra S6 metric. Hint ladder again.

source: Han et al. (2025) Creativity or Brute Force? Using Brainteasers as a Window into LLM Problem-Solving
finding: Rewriting narrative brainteasers into competition-style math raised accuracy; models accept a wrong 'correction' when told to.
numbers: 30 rewritten Math problems: o3 56.7% -> 73.3% (p=0.023); deepseek-reasoner 50.0% -> 63.3% (p=0.043); R1-Distill-Llama-70B 23.3% -> 33.3% (p=0.08). Swap test: models accepted a false correction of the correct solution over 60% of the time; justified denial very rare. 3 of 6 models gave valid corrections in over 80% of cases.
limits: n=30 rewrites; 14 flawed examples inspected in the correction test.
agent_relevance: Restating a problem in formal form (our restate operator) has measured value. Models defer to a stated answer, supporting G5 (judges see no proposed answer).

source: Han et al. (2025) Creativity or Brute Force? Using Brainteasers as a Window into LLM Problem-Solving
finding: o3 used the most informative hint last because the hint was long.
numbers: Case study: six-digit number puzzle; hints ranked by surface length, giving a far larger candidate list than the human solution.
limits: Single case study.
agent_relevance: Diagnostic for test sets: hint ordering. Operators should rank cues by information, not length (G5 length bias).

source: Wadhwa et al. (2026) CREATE: Testing LLMs for Associative Creativity
finding: Benchmark of associative paths between concepts scored for specificity and diversity; thinking models are not always better and creative prompting gives limited gains.
numbers: No numbers read (abstract page only).
limits: Only the abstract page was read; no tables.
agent_relevance: Thinking budget and creativity prompts do not guarantee better association quality; read the full paper before relying on it.
